sample.universe: The entire Danish population; children enrolled in public schools in mainstream classrooms who took the National Test in reading or math in spring 2010-2013
sample.unit_of_observation: Pupil observed in a school-cohort (school x grade x year), with a base-year and an end-year test score
selection_rules: Select children enrolled in public schools in mainstream classrooms who took the National Test in reading or math in the relevant years

Keep only cohorts from schools where at least some of the students continued at the same school until the end year, which excludes cohorts from schools that close and from small schools that did not offer the relevant grades
Remove very small school-cohorts (less than 10 pupils) and very large ones (more than 200 pupils)
Exclude the potentially disruptive students who move and thereby create the identifying variation, so their test scores are not in the analysis
Use only children with test scores in both the base year (2010 or 2011) and the end year (2012 or 2013)
sample.n_observations: Reading: 238,795 (divorced-parents sample), 237,815 (criminal-parents sample), 246,022 (psychiatric-diagnosis sample); math: 38,272 / 38,199 / 39,552; SDQ survey subsample: 9516; Table 1 means column: 246,590

construction_notes: Parents are defined as divorced if they do not live at the same address on January 1 in the year the child turns 5; marriage and cohabitation are not distinguished
Parents are defined as criminal if the father or the mother was convicted of a non-traffic crime, or sentenced to prison for a sufficiently severe traffic-related crime, before the child turns 6
Children with a psychiatric diagnosis are those with registered psychiatric diagnoses at general hospitals before age 9 (age 5 in the Table 5 column 7 robustness check)
All other child and parent information is measured at age 5, the year before school start

Test scores: each of the three profile areas is standardized within grade-year, averaged, and the average standardized again within grade-year, so the test score has mean zero and standard deviation one
The National Test ability measures are distributed from -7 to 7 on a logit scale before standardization
Disrupt and Movement are 0/1 indicators of entry and exit rather than changes in fractions, which allows asymmetries and non-linearities
Variation is taken at the school-cohort level rather than the classroom level
Gross income is measured in 2000 prices, in 100,000 DKK
Reading tests are two years apart (2nd/4th/6th grade in the base year); math tests are three years apart (3rd grade 2010 and 6th grade 2013)

claims.statement: Receiving a child with divorced parents in the school-cohort lowers peers' reading test score by 0.0023 standard deviations (Table 3, Panel A, column (4): full model: school fixed effects, school-cohort characteristics and individual characteristics).

treatment.label: Increase of children with divorced parents in the school-cohort (0/1)

definition.value: Indicator taking the value one if at least one child whose parents had divorced before the child turned 6 (parents are defined as divorced if they do not live at the same address on January 1 in the year the child turns 5) entered the pupil's school-cohort since t-1, i.e. between the base-year and the end-year National Test; the counterfactual is receipt of a non-disruptive child. Variation is taken at the school-cohort (school x grade x year) level, not the classroom level, and the disruptive movers' own test scores are excluded from the estimation sample.

timing.value: Movement measured between the base-year test (spring 2010 or 2011) and the end-year test (spring 2012 or 2013); the disruptiveness characteristic itself is measured before school start (divorce/crime, by age 5-6) or before age 9 (psychiatric diagnosis).

outcome.label: Test score in reading (z-score), end year

definition.value: Individual score on the National Test in reading in the end year. One test score is constructed as a standardized average of the scores across the three profile areas: the score of each profile area is standardized for each grade-year combination, averaged, and the average standardized again for each grade-year combination so that the test score has mean zero and standard deviation one. The base-year reading score enters the model as a control, so the parameter is a value-added (test-score gain) effect.

timing.value: End-year National Test in reading (spring 2012 or 2013), two years after the base-year test (2nd, 4th or 6th grade in spring 2010 or 2011).

units.value: standard deviations of the within grade-year standardized test score

estimand.target_population: Peers - the non-moving pupils - in Danish public-school cohorts that receive an additional child
estimand.time_horizon: Test score measured at the end-year National Test, two years after the base-year test; the paper calls it the pupils' immediate academic achievement.
estimand.formal_query: E[y_ict | do(Disrupt_ct = 1)] - E[y_ict | do(Disrupt_ct = 0)] with the counterfactual being receipt of a non-disruptive child, for pupils in the receiving school-cohort, conditional on y_ic,t-1 and the conditioning set

population.selection: Conditioned on having a National Test score in reading in both the base year and the end year; children exempted from the test are not observed; the potentially disruptive children who move, and who generate the identifying variation, are excluded from the estimation sample; very small (<10) and very large (>200) school-cohorts and cohorts at schools where no student continued to the end year are removed.

identification.source_of_variation: Children who move between schools and thereby generate variation in peer composition in the receiving school-cohort, between the base-year and the end-year National Test.

key_assumptions.assumption: Given the conditioning set - lagged test score, school fixed effects, school-cohort characteristics and individual and family background - the influx of potentially disruptive children is unrelated to changes in the peers' test scores. In the value added framework the movement of pupils need only be exogenous to changes in test scores, not to levels.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1: linear probability models of each influx dummy on the whole conditioning set; the coefficients are small relative to mean values, the signs show no particular type of selection, and the influx is unrelated to base-year test score levels. Also the future-movements falsification test in Table 5, column 8.

key_assumptions.assumption: Value-added functional restriction: the lagged test score enters linearly with a freely estimated coefficient delta, rather than being restricted to delta = 1 as in a gain-score model.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

unresolved_confounders: Aids and assistance given to children during the National Test are not observed and cannot be controlled for.
The authors cannot completely rule out that teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class during the test.
Children exempted from the test are not observed, so the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.

mediators_claimed: Behaviour of the entering child: the primary channel is thought to be through behavior, documented by the relationship between the disruptiveness indicators and the SDQ total difficulties score in Table 2

heterogeneity.dimension: gender of the entering disruptive child
heterogeneity.finding: An influx of boys with divorced parents has a negative effect on peers' test scores (-0.0147, s.e. 0.0068) whereas an influx of girls with divorced parents does not (-0.0020, s.e. 0.0075); the paper notes the two estimates are not statistically different from each other (Table 4).

heterogeneity.dimension: grade level in the base year
heterogeneity.finding: Effects are generally bigger when the disruptive child moves into the classroom between 4th and 6th grade, and the effect of receiving a child with a psychiatric diagnosis between 4th and 6th grade is significant at the 5% level; in general the paper cannot reject that the effects are equal across grade levels (results available upon request).

heterogeneity.dimension: gender of the affected peer
heterogeneity.finding: Models estimated separately for female and male peers; the paper cannot reject the null hypothesis that disruptive children affect girls as much as boys (results available upon request).

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

claims.statement: Receiving a child with criminal parents in the school-cohort lowers peers' reading test score by 0.0289 standard deviations (Table 3, Panel B, column (1): no school fixed effects: movement dummies and baseline test scores only).

treatment.label: Increase of children with criminal parents in the school-cohort (0/1)

definition.value: Indicator taking the value one if at least one child whose father or mother had been convicted of a non-traffic crime, or sentenced to prison for a sufficiently severe traffic-related crime, before the child turned 6 entered the pupil's school-cohort since t-1, i.e. between the base-year and the end-year National Test; the counterfactual is receipt of a non-disruptive child. Variation is taken at the school-cohort (school x grade x year) level, not the classroom level, and the disruptive movers' own test scores are excluded from the estimation sample.

timing.value: Movement measured between the base-year test (spring 2010 or 2011) and the end-year test (spring 2012 or 2013); the disruptiveness characteristic itself is measured before school start (divorce/crime, by age 5-6) or before age 9 (psychiatric diagnosis).

outcome.label: Test score in reading (z-score), end year

definition.value: Individual score on the National Test in reading in the end year. One test score is constructed as a standardized average of the scores across the three profile areas: the score of each profile area is standardized for each grade-year combination, averaged, and the average standardized again for each grade-year combination so that the test score has mean zero and standard deviation one. The base-year reading score enters the model as a control, so the parameter is a value-added (test-score gain) effect.

timing.value: End-year National Test in reading (spring 2012 or 2013), two years after the base-year test (2nd, 4th or 6th grade in spring 2010 or 2011).

units.value: standard deviations of the within grade-year standardized test score

estimand.target_population: Peers - the non-moving pupils - in Danish public-school cohorts that receive an additional child
estimand.time_horizon: Test score measured at the end-year National Test, two years after the base-year test; the paper calls it the pupils' immediate academic achievement.

population.description: Pupils enrolled in Danish public schools in mainstream classrooms who took the National Test in reading in both the base year (spring 2010 or 2011) and the end year (spring 2012 or 2013), in school-cohorts of between 10 and 200 pupils at schools where at least some students continued at the same school until the end year.

definition.value: Indicator taking the value one if at least one child whose father or mother had been convicted of a non-traffic crime, or sentenced to prison for a sufficiently severe traffic-related crime, before the child turned 6 entered the pupil's school-cohort since t-1, i.e. between the base-year and the end-year National Test; the counterfactual is receipt of a non-disruptive child. Variation is taken at the school-cohort (school x grade x year) level, not the classroom level, and the disruptive movers' own test scores are excluded from the estimation sample.

timing.value: Movement measured between the base-year test (spring 2010 or 2011) and the end-year test (spring 2012 or 2013); the disruptiveness characteristic itself is measured before school start (divorce/crime, by age 5-6) or before age 9 (psychiatric diagnosis).

outcome.label: Test score in reading (z-score), end year

definition.value: Individual score on the National Test in reading in the end year. One test score is constructed as a standardized average of the scores across the three profile areas: the score of each profile area is standardized for each grade-year combination, averaged, and the average standardized again for each grade-year combination so that the test score has mean zero and standard deviation one. The base-year reading score enters the model as a control, so the parameter is a value-added (test-score gain) effect.

timing.value: End-year National Test in reading (spring 2012 or 2013), two years after the base-year test (2nd, 4th or 6th grade in spring 2010 or 2011).

units.value: standard deviations of the within grade-year standardized test score

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

treatment.label: Decrease of any children in the school-cohort (0/1)

definition.value: Element of the 1 x 2 vector Movement, which registers any movement into or out of the school-cohort: the indicator equals one if any child left the school-cohort since t-1, disruptive or not.

timing.value: Movement measured between the base-year test (spring 2010 or 2011) and the end-year test (spring 2012 or 2013).

outcome.label: Test score in reading (z-score), end year

definition.value: Individual score on the National Test in reading in the end year. units.value: standard deviations of the within grade-year standardized test score

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

claims.statement: Increase of girls with divorced parents in the school-cohort (0/1) is associated with a change of -0.0020 standard deviations in Test score in reading (z-score), end year (Table 4, column 'Divorced parents', row 'Increase of girls').

treatment.label: Increase of girls with divorced parents in the school-cohort (0/1)

definition.value: Indicator taking the value one if at least one child whose parents had divorced before the child turned 6 (parents are defined as divorced if they do not live at the same address on January 1 in the year the child turns 5), of the female sex, entered the pupil's school-cohort since t-1; the model includes the disruption and movement dummies separately by the gender of the moving children.

timing.value: Movement measured between the base-year test (spring 2010 or 2011) and the end-year test (spring 2012 or 2013); the disruptiveness characteristic itself is measured before school start (divorce/crime, by age 5-6) or before age 9 (psychiatric diagnosis).

outcome.label: Test score in reading (z-score), end year

definition.value: Individual score on the National Test in reading in the end year. One test score is constructed as a standardized average of the scores across the three profile areas: the score of each profile area is standardized for each grade-year combination, averaged, and the average standardized again for each grade-year combination so that the test score has mean zero and standard deviation one. The base-year reading score enters the model as a control, so the parameter is a value-added (test-score gain) effect.

timing.value: End-year National Test in reading (spring 2012 or 2013), two years after the base-year test (2nd, 4th or 6th grade in spring 2010 or 2011).

units.value: standard deviations of the within grade-year standardized test score

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

claims.statement: Increase of children with a psychiatric diagnosis in the school-cohort (0/1) is associated with a change of -0.0182 standard deviations in Test score in reading (z-score), end year (Table 5, column (3) 'Sibling fixed effect', row 'Increase' for children with a psychiatric diagnosis).

treatment.label: Increase of children with a psychiatric diagnosis in the school-cohort (0/1)

definition.value: Indicator taking the value one if at least one child with a psychiatric diagnosis registered at a general hospital before age 9 entered the pupil's school-cohort since t-1, i.e. between the base-year and the end-year National Test; the counterfactual is receipt of a non-disruptive child. Variation is taken at the school-cohort (school x grade x year) level, not the classroom level, and the disruptive movers' own test scores are excluded from the estimation sample.

timing.value: Movement measured between the base-year test (spring 2010 or 2011) and the end-year test (spring 2012 or 2013); the disruptiveness characteristic itself is measured before school start (divorce/crime, by age 5-6) or before age 9 (psychiatric diagnosis).

outcome.label: Test score in reading (z-score), end year

definition.value: Individual score on the National Test in reading in the end year. One test score is constructed as a standardized average of the scores across the three profile areas: the score of each profile area is standardized for each grade-year combination, averaged, and the average standardized again for each grade-year combination so that the test score has mean zero and standard deviation one. The base-year reading score enters the model as a control, so the parameter is a value-added (test-score gain) effect.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

claims.statement: Increase of children with a psychiatric diagnosis in the school-cohort (0/1) is associated with a change of -0.0448 standard deviations in Test score in reading (z-score), end year (Table 5, column (6) 'Movers who moved municipality', row 'Increase' for children with a psychiatric diagnosis).

treatment.label: Increase of children with a psychiatric diagnosis in the school-cohort (0/1)

definition.value: Indicator taking the value one if at least one child with a psychiatric diagnosis registered at a general hospital before age 9 entered the pupil's school-cohort since t-1, i.e. between the base-year and the end-year National Test; the counterfactual is receipt of a non-disruptive child. Variation is taken at the school-cohort (school x grade x year) level, not the classroom level, and the disruptive movers' own test scores are excluded from the estimation sample.

timing.value: Movement measured between the base-year test (spring 2010 or 2011) and the end-year test (spring 2012 or 2013); the disruptiveness characteristic itself is measured before school start (divorce/crime, by age 5-6) or before age 9 (psychiatric diagnosis).

outcome.label: Test score in reading (z-score), end year

definition.value: Individual score on the National Test in reading in the end year. One test score is constructed as a standardized average of the scores across the three profile areas: the score of each profile area is standardized for each grade-year combination, averaged, and the average standardized again for each grade-year combination so that the test score has mean zero and standard deviation one. The base-year reading score enters the model as a control, so the parameter is a value-added (test-score gain) effect.

timing.value: End-year National Test in reading (spring 2012 or 2013), two years after the base-year test (2nd, 4th or 6th grade in spring 2010 or 2011).

units.value: standard deviations of the within grade-year standardized test score

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.

Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

threats_discussed: Teachers may assist weak children or give aids during the test; this is unobserved. Teachers in classes that receive a disruptive child may compensate by giving more aid to the rest of the class, biasing the results toward zero, or may spend all their time on the disruptive child, biasing them the other way.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.
The school principal might sort new students across classrooms and teachers on unobservable criteria, which is why variation is taken at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level.

Variation is at the school-cohort rather than the classroom level: if disruptive behaviour only affects students in the same classroom, the estimated effect is downward biased by the unaffected classrooms.
Headmasters may exempt students from the test, and exempted children are typically children who would perform poorly; the effect on the worst-performing children may not be captured.
Parents may strategically settle in school districts where they believe the children are less likely to affect the new peers, which would bias the results.

Conditioning on future movements (column 8 of Table 5) corresponds in some sense to conditioning on an outcome, because influx of potentially disruptive children today could affect future movements out of the classroom.

population.description: Pupils in the main reading sample; the unit is the pupil, and the dependent variable is whether the pupil's school-cohort received a potentially disruptive child between the base-year and the end-year test.
population.ages: Pupils in 2nd, 4th or 6th grade in the base year and in 4th, 6th or 8th grade in the end year
population.selection: Conditioned on having a National Test score in reading in both the base year and the end year; children exempted from the test are not observed; the potentially disruptive children who move, and who generate the identifying variation, are excluded from the estimation sample; very small (<10) and very large (>200) school-cohorts and cohorts at schools where no student continued to the end year are removed.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-school variation in pupil background characteristics and base-year test scores; the regression is a balance / predictability check.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditioning variables are predetermined with respect to the influx: all child and parent information is measured at age 5, the year before school start, so that school experiences do not influence the background characteristics.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Timing of the variables.

implies_edges.from: School experiences after enrolment
implies_edges.to: Background characteristics measured at age 5

key_assumptions.assumption: This is a predictability check rather than a causal estimate: the model is meant to show how well the increases can be predicted by characteristics of the school-cohort, i.e. to what extent the influx is an exogenous shock to the peer composition.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated purpose of the exercise.

threats_discussed: With more than 200,000 observations occasional significance is expected, so the authors read the size of the estimates relative to mean values rather than their significance.
robustness_checks: An alternative version regressing each individual characteristic on the disruption-increase dummies gives qualitatively the same conclusions (available upon request)

estimator.value: OLS linear probability model; the table reports marginal effects evaluated at the mean

estimation.specification: Linear probability model of the disruption-increase dummy on the full conditioning set (33 child, mother, father, grade and base-year variables) and school fixed effects.
controls: Child background measured at age 5: psychiatric diagnosis at age 5, divorced parents, parents who committed non-traffic crime, parents who committed violent crime or have been to prison, immigrant, birth weight less than 1500 g, birth weight 1500-2500 g, male, APGAR5 not 10

Mother measured when the child is 5: number of older siblings, age, degree of unemployment, gross income (2000 prices, in 100,000 DKK), education (high school, vocational, 2-year college, 4-year college, MSc or PhD)
Father measured when the child is 5: age, degree of unemployment, gross income (2000 prices, in 100,000 DKK), education (high school, vocational, 2-year college, 4-year college, MSc or PhD)

estimation.clustering: Standard errors clustered at the school level

claims.statement: The individual level background characteristics are jointly significant predictors of the influx of children with a psychiatric diagnosis into the school-cohort (Table 1, column 3: F-test p-value 0.0236).

treatment.label: Individual level background characteristics (joint F-test)

definition.value: Joint F-test of the child, mother and father background variables listed in Table 1 - the variables above the grade and BaseYear dummies - in the linear probability model for the influx dummy; the table row is 'F-test variables above without grade and BaseYear (p-value)'.

timing.value: All child and parent information is measured at age 5, the year before school start.

outcome.label: Increase of children with a psychiatric diagnosis in the school-cohort (0/1)

definition.value: Dependent variable of the linear probability model in Table 1: indicator equal to one if at least one child with a psychiatric diagnosis registered at a general hospital before age 9 entered the pupil's school-cohort since t-1.

timing.value: Movement between the base-year test (spring 2010 or 2011) and the end-year test (spring 2012 or 2013).

magnitude.interpretation: There may be some correlation with regards to the influx of children with a psychiatric diagnosis (the text reports 0.024).
